title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM MOSES IN MIDIAN
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM MOSES IN MIDIAN
Some of the most important seasons of your life will feel like God forgot you.
Just another ordinary day that looks exactly like yesterday.
That is where Moses found himself.
And that is where I found myself too.
For years, I misunderstood the story of Midian. I thought Moses was waiting there. I thought God had placed him on pause. I thought the wilderness was simply a holding room before destiny arrived.
But Scripture tells a different story.
Midian was not where Moses wasted forty years.
Midian was where God rewrote him.
The Moses who fled Egypt was not the Moses who stood before Pharaoh.
The Moses who killed a man was not the Moses who delivered a nation.
The Moses who arrived in Midian was driven by anger, impulse, self-confidence, and human strength.
The Moses who left Midian carried something entirely different.
That realization changed the way I view every painful season of my life.
Because many of us are trying to escape the very place where God is trying to transform us.
Moses had grown up in Pharaoh's palace. Educated. Powerful. Privileged.
He knew God had a purpose.
But instead of waiting for God's timing, he tried to accomplish God's mission through human effort.
When he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew slave, Moses killed the Egyptian and buried him in the sand (Exodus 2:12).
The Hebrew text says Moses fled to the land of Midian.
Midian was not the Promised Land.
At least it seemed that way.
Have you ever felt like that?
Too far from where you used to be.
Too far from where you think God wants you to go.
Stuck in a place that feels disconnected from purpose.
And many believers are living there right now.
The place where life did not go according to plan.
Yet God specializes in meeting people there.
The remarkable thing is that Scripture records almost nothing dramatic during Moses' forty years in Midian.
The number alone should stop us.
Forty years is longer than many careers.
Longer than many people's entire walk with Christ.
Yet God considered every one of those years necessary.
That truth confronts our modern obsession with speed.
The wilderness is where roots grow.
Moses is tending sheep when he sees a bush burning without being consumed.
The Hebrew word used for bush is "seneh" (סְנֶה).
A small, seemingly insignificant desert shrub.
God often chooses ordinary things to reveal extraordinary glory.
As Moses approaches, God calls his name.
God was not calling a prophet.
A shepherd who likely believed his greatest opportunities were behind him.
"Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground."
The ground was not holy because of its geography.
It became holy because God was there.
The wilderness became sacred when God's presence arrived.
That means your Midian can become holy too.
The place you want to leave.
The place you pray God will remove.
It may be the very place where God reveals Himself most clearly.
One detail in Exodus 3 has always gripped my heart.
"I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob."
The Hebrew phrase "Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh" (אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה), later translated "I AM WHO I AM," appears in this encounter.
The verb "ehyeh" carries the sense of continual existence and faithful presence.
God was telling Moses something profound.
I was faithful before you failed.
I was faithful while you were running.
I was faithful during every silent year.
And I will be faithful after this moment.
Your failure does not interrupt God's faithfulness.
Your weakness does not cancel His promises.
Your mistakes do not erase His plans.
The greatest lesson I learned from Moses in Midian is this:
God is more interested in who you are becoming than where you currently are.
Before Moses could confront Pharaoh, pride had to die.
Before Moses could lead millions, self-reliance had to die.
Before Moses could carry God's authority, dependence on God had to be born.
Midian accomplished what Egypt never could.
And paradoxically, that breaking became his greatest qualification.
Years later, Scripture describes Moses as very humble, more than all men on the face of the earth (Numbers 12:3).
That man was not created in Pharaoh's palace.
Perhaps that is why some of God's deepest work feels painful.
Because He is not merely improving us.
The Greek New Testament uses the word "metamorphoō" (μεταμορφόω) for transformation.
It is the same root from which we derive the word metamorphosis.
God does not simply renovate people.
That process often happens in hidden places.
Looking back, I realize my own Midian seasons were not punishments.
The loneliness taught intimacy with God.
And perhaps you are discovering the same thing right now.
Perhaps you are standing in a Midian season wondering why God feels silent.
Maybe you are asking the same questions Moses likely asked.
Why has it taken so long?
The answer may be simpler than you think.
God is still writing the story.
The beauty of the Gospel is that God specializes in rewriting stories.
Yet Jesus transformed every one of those stories.
That is the heartbeat of our mission.
The cross itself proves this truth.
What appeared to be defeat became victory.
What appeared to be shame became glory.
What appeared to be an ending became the beginning of redemption.
The Greek word Christ cried from the cross, "Tetelestai" (Τετέλεσται), means "It is finished" or "It has been accomplished."
Because of Jesus, no wilderness is wasted.
And one day, often when you least expect it, God will call your name.
You will realize He was present the entire time.
Because He loved you enough to prepare you.
If this story stirred something in your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Your testimony may become someone else's encouragement.
Because sometimes the place that feels furthest from your destiny is actually the place where God is preparing you for it.
The wilderness was never the end of Moses' story.
And it is not the end of yours.
The God who met Moses in Midian still meets people in impossible places today.
And Jesus is still rewriting stories.
The place you wanted to escape may become the testimony you one day thank God for.
